newsitem.title: GERMANY: FOCUS - Dresdner optimistic, but sees tough 97.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - Dresdner optimistic, but sees tough 97.

text.p: Germany's second largest commercial bank Dresdner Bank AG said on Thursday it had got off to a good start in the first two months of the year and was optimistic for 1997 despite tough operating conditions ahead.

The bank, the last of the Big Five to report 1996 profits, put its rivals in the shade with a 31 percent surge in net profit in the year which marked the first full-year consolidation of London-based investment bank Kleinwort Benson.

Chairman Juergen Sarrazin told a news conference the uptrend continued into 1997 with operating profit before risk provisions up at least 10 percent in the first two months, although this could not be extrapolated for the full year.

"The business environment will remain difficult for German banks in 1997," he said, warning that the insolvency crisis among Germany's mid-sized firms would keep provisions against lending losses high, albeit stable.

But good capital market conditions would boost securities income and Sarrazin told a news conference he expected "a 1997 profit that will allow us both to pay a shareholder-friendly dividend and further strengthen internal reserves."

The bank's net profit surged to 1.58 billion marks ($917 million) in 1996 while operating earnings advanced 44 percent to 2.86 billion, after what Sarrazin said was a "significant boost" to interest and commission income in the final quarter.

Analysts speculated that the late boost could be related to the massive Deutsche Telekom flotation in November, for which Dresdner acted as a global co-ordinator. Dresdner itself refused to specify how much it earned from the issue.

Loan loss provisions for 1996 rose 2.4 percent to 1.1 billion marks while lending volume surged 16 percent to 322.8 billion. Net interest income rose 9.5 percent while commission income surged 35.5 percent to 4.13 billion marks.

Earlier this week, Dresdner's supervisory board approved the bank's plans to raise its dividend payout to 1.45 marks a share from 1.35 marks and to pay a ten-pfennig bonus dividend per share to mark its 125th anniversary.

The figures, broad estimates of which had already been released, had minimal impact on Dresdner's shares, which fell in line with a trend in the banking sector to end Thursday's bourse session down 78 pfennigs at 57.92 marks.
But the bank's results surpassed those achieved by its main rivals, with Commerzbank AG, ranked third by asset volume, coming closest with a 24 percent net earnings rise.

Sarrazin said the Dresdner's investment banking business, to which it has committed considerable funds in its bid to become a global player, had contributed at least 100 million marks to group earnings in the past year.

But Sarrazin said there was room for improvement in the structure of Dresdner's earnings: "Last year our commission income was 60 percent of our net result, compared with around 38 percent five years ago. We want to pursue this direction."

Expanding investment banking and asset management is at the core of this strategy and Dresdner has created a new organisational structure for its investment banking business, which will be run from London and Frankfurt and supervised by a council of management board members and regional unit managers.

Within that structure, global corporate finance and equities will be run from London, global markets (fixed income) will be run from Frankfurt and global finance will be divided between the two centres.
The company has also created a San Francisco-based umbrella group, Dresdner RCM Global Investors, to head its institutional asset management activities outside Germany.

The group is led by newly-acquired fund group RCM Capital Management, which was consolidated into group results as of June and brings Dresdner's total assets under management, counting private assets, to 330 billion marks. Dresdner said it has set itself a target to boost its return on own equity, now 11.5 percent after tax and 20 percent before tax to 15 percent and 25 percent respectively.

The bank also means to continue to expand in asset management and remains on the lookout for suitable targets, especialy in the U.K. and Europe. "There will certainly be changes from the present situation," Sarrazin said. ($ = 1.722 German Marks)
